```{r setup}
library(birdnetR)
```

The `birdnetR` package lets you use the `birdnet` Python package from R. This guide shows how to load models, identify species in audio files, predict species for a location, extract embeddings, and run custom classifiers.


##  Installation

Install the released version from CRAN:

```r
install.packages("birdnetR")
```
<br>
or install the development version from GitHub with:

```r
pak::pak("birdnet-team/birdnetR")
```
<br>

<div style="padding: 15px; margin-bottom: 20px; border: 1px solid #bce8f1; border-radius: 4px; background-color: #d9edf7; color: #31708f;">
<strong>Note</strong><br>
 You don't need to install Python yourself. `birdnetR` uses [`reticulate::py_require()`](https://rstudio.github.io/reticulate/reference/py_require.html) to set up Python and the `birdnet` package the first time you use it. This takes a few minutes once. The default setup is small: TensorFlow or PyTorch are downloaded only when you first load a model that needs them (see [Choosing a model](#choosing-a-model)).
</div>


## Usage

### Load a BirdNET model
To begin, load a model. On first use, the model files are downloaded; after that they are read from disk.

```{r init_model}
# BirdNET+ V3.0 acoustic model (the default)
model <- birdnet_load()
#> BirdNET acoustic 3.0 · onnx · fp32 · en_us · 11,725 classes
```

Every load prints one line: the model, its backend, precision, language and number of classes. Use `suppressMessages(birdnet_load())` to load quietly. `print(model)` shows the same line again.

BirdNET+ V3.0 recognises about 11,700 classes, including many non-bird animals such as frogs, insects and mammals. The exact number depends on the release of the model.


### Identify species in an audio file
`birdnet_predict()` runs the model on one or more audio files. It returns a prediction object that you convert to a data frame with `as.data.frame()`. Each row is one detection in one segment of the recording (3 seconds by default).

```{r species_in_audio}
# Path to an example audio file (replace with your own file path)
audio_path <- system.file("extdata", "soundscape.mp3", package = "birdnetR")

# Predict species in the audio file
predictions <- birdnet_predict(model, audio_path, min_confidence = 0.3)

# Convert to a data frame
df <- as.data.frame(predictions)
head(df)

# Example output (the input column holds the full file path):
#>            input start_time end_time                                species_name confidence
#> 1 soundscape.mp3          0        3 Poecile atricapillus_Black-capped Chickadee  0.9206197
#> 2 soundscape.mp3          0        3            Haemorhous mexicanus_House Finch  0.3681544
#> 3 soundscape.mp3          3        6 Poecile atricapillus_Black-capped Chickadee  0.7824634
#> 4 soundscape.mp3          6        9            Haemorhous mexicanus_House Finch  0.5423213
#> 5 soundscape.mp3          6        9              Junco hyemalis_Dark-eyed Junco  0.5064150
#> 6 soundscape.mp3          9       12            Haemorhous mexicanus_House Finch  0.9012285
```

The columns are:

- `input`: the audio file,
- `start_time`, `end_time`: the segment, in seconds from the start of the file,
- `species_name`: scientific and common name, separated by an underscore,
- `confidence`: the score (see `?birdnet_predict.birdnet_model_acoustic` on how to read it).

If several species score above `min_confidence` in the same segment, you get one row per species (at most `top_k`, default 5; `top_k = NULL` returns all of them).

Pass a vector of paths to analyse several files in one call:

```{r several_files}
files <- list.files("recordings", pattern = "\\.wav$", full.names = TRUE)
predictions <- birdnet_predict(model, files)
```

To process many files and save the results, see the [workflow article](workflow.html).


### Using a custom species list
Often you only need some of the species the model knows. Pass a custom species list to limit the output to those species.

Class labels consist of the scientific name and the common name, separated by an underscore, like this:
```{r class_label_example}
"Agelaius phoeniceus_Red-winged Blackbird"
"Cyanocitta cristata_Blue Jay"
```

Get the full species list of a loaded model with `birdnet_list_species()`:

```{r species_list}
species <- birdnet_list_species(model)
head(species)
```

Every name must be in the model's species list, otherwise `birdnet_predict()` stops with an error. Names can differ between model versions. For example, Cooper's Hawk is `Accipiter cooperii` in BirdNET V2.4 and `Astur cooperii` in V3.0. Always take the names from the model you use.

To filter predictions to specific species, pass a character vector to the `species_list` argument:

```{r use_custom_species_list}
predictions <- birdnet_predict(model, audio_path,
  species_list = c("Cyanocitta cristata_Blue Jay", "Junco hyemalis_Dark-eyed Junco"),
  min_confidence = 0.3
)

as.data.frame(predictions)
```


### BirdNET V2.4 and Perch v2

BirdNET V2.4 is the model that birdnetR 0.x used. It has 6,522 classes and runs on the default installation:

```{r model_24}
model_24 <- birdnet_load(version = "2.4")
#> BirdNET acoustic 2.4 · tf/litert · fp32 · en_us · 6,522 classes
```

[Perch v2](https://www.kaggle.com/models/google/bird-vocalization-classifier) is an acoustic model by Google with 14,795 classes (birds and other animals). It analyses 5-second segments.

```{r perch}
perch <- birdnet_load_perch()
#> Perch v2 · pb · CPU · 14,795 classes

predictions <- birdnet_predict(perch, audio_path)
```

Perch needs TensorFlow. birdnetR installs it the first time you load Perch, which downloads about 600 MB. Perch does not run on Intel Macs.

Perch scores are raw model outputs (logits), not values between 0 and 1. They are not comparable with BirdNET scores, and the default `min_confidence = 0.1` has a different meaning for them. Use `apply_sigmoid = TRUE` or `apply_softmax = TRUE` in `birdnet_predict()` if you need scores between 0 and 1.

Perch's species names are scientific names only (for example `"Poecile atricapillus"`), so `birdnet_load_perch()` has no `language` argument.


### Predict species occurrence with the geo model
BirdNET includes a geographic model that predicts which species are likely to occur at a location and week of the year. It returns a prediction object with species names and scores.

BirdNET's year has 48 weeks: four per month, so week 1 is the first week of January and week 48 the last week of December.

```{r use_geo_model}
# Load the geo model
geo_model <- birdnet_load(type = "geo")

# Predict species occurrence in Ithaca, NY in week 4 (the end of January)
predictions <- birdnet_predict(geo_model, latitude = 42.5, longitude = -76.45, week = 4L)

# Convert to a data frame and sort by score
df <- as.data.frame(predictions)
head(df[order(-df$confidence), ])

# Example output:
#>                           species_name confidence
#>     Spinus tristis_American Goldfinch  0.9998151
#>        Junco hyemalis_Dark-eyed Junco  0.9997241
#>  Dryobates pubescens_Downy Woodpecker  0.9997090
#>        Zenaida macroura_Mourning Dove  0.9996312
```

With `week = NULL` (the default), the model predicts for the whole year. `year_round_aggregation` then decides how the weekly scores are combined: `"max"` (the default) or `"average"`.

```{r geo_year_round}
predictions <- birdnet_predict(geo_model, latitude = 42.5, longitude = -76.45)
```

You can use the geo prediction as a species list for the acoustic model. Every name in `species_list` must be in the acoustic model, so keep only the shared names, and use geo and acoustic models of the same version:

```{r geo_species_list}
local_species <- as.data.frame(predictions)$species_name
local_species <- intersect(local_species, birdnet_list_species(model))
predictions <- birdnet_predict(model, audio_path, species_list = local_species)
```


### Translating common species names

Common names are available in several languages. The two model versions support different languages:
```{r languages}
birdnet_list_languages()      # BirdNET+ V3.0
birdnet_list_languages("2.4") # BirdNET V2.4
```

To get common names in your preferred language, load the model with the `language` argument:
```{r}
model_fr <- birdnet_load(language = "fr")

# Get species list in French
head(birdnet_list_species(model_fr))
```


### Extract embeddings

Embeddings are the feature vectors a model computes for each audio segment before it scores the species. You can use them for clustering, similarity search or to train your own classifier.

```{r encode}
embeddings <- birdnet_encode(model, audio_path)
df <- as.data.frame(embeddings)
```

The data frame has the columns `input`, `start_time`, `end_time` and `embedding`. `embedding` is a list column with one numeric vector per segment (1,280 values for BirdNET+ V3.0, 1,024 for V2.4). To get a matrix with one row per segment:

```{r embedding_matrix}
emb <- do.call(rbind, df$embedding)
dim(emb)
```

`birdnet_write(embeddings, "embeddings.parquet")` saves them to a file.


### Custom classifiers

You can train your own classifier with [BirdNET-Analyzer](https://github.com/birdnet-team/BirdNET-Analyzer) on top of BirdNET V2.4 or V3.0. BirdNET-Analyzer exports a TFLite file and a species list (labels) file.

`birdnet_inspect_custom()` describes a TFLite classifier without loading it:

```{r inspect_custom}
info <- birdnet_inspect_custom("/path/to/CustomClassifier.tflite")
str(info)
#> List of 6
#>  $ version          : chr "2.4"
#>  $ mode             : chr "replace"
#>  $ n_species        : int 345
#>  $ applies_sigmoid  : logi FALSE
#>  $ supports_encoding: logi TRUE
#>  $ input_samples    : int 144000
```

- `version`: the base model, `"2.4"` or `"3.0"`.
- `mode`: `"replace"` (only your classes) or `"append"` (your classes added to the base model's).
- `n_species`: the number of classes.
- `applies_sigmoid`: whether the model applies the sigmoid itself.
- `supports_encoding`: whether `birdnet_encode()` works with it.
- `input_samples`: the number of audio samples per segment (`NULL` if any length is accepted).

To load it, give the paths to the model file and the species list file. birdnetR reads the base version from the file:

```{r init_custom_model}
custom_model <- birdnet_load_custom(
  model = "/path/to/CustomClassifier.tflite",
  species_list = "/path/to/CustomClassifier_Labels.txt"
)

predictions <- birdnet_predict(custom_model, audio_path)
```

TFLite classifiers on the V2.4 base run on the default installation. For a Raven export (a folder) or another Protobuf classifier, set `backend = "pb"` and the base version, because it can't be read from the files. This installs TensorFlow on first use:

```{r raven}
raven_model <- birdnet_load_custom(
  model = "/path/to/raven_export",
  species_list = "/path/to/raven_labels.csv",
  version = "2.4",
  backend = "pb",
  is_raven = TRUE
)
```

Raven exports can't be used with `birdnet_encode()`.


## Choosing a model

| Model | Load with | Classes | License of the model files |
|---|---|---|---|
| BirdNET+ V3.0 acoustic (default) | `birdnet_load()` | about 11,700 | Apache 2.0 |
| BirdNET+ V3.0 geo | `birdnet_load(type = "geo")` | about 14,000 | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 |
| BirdNET V2.4 acoustic | `birdnet_load(version = "2.4")` | 6,522 | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 |
| BirdNET V2.4 geo | `birdnet_load(type = "geo", version = "2.4")` | 6,522 | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 |
| Perch v2 (Google) | `birdnet_load_perch()` | 14,795 | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 |

CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 allows non-commercial use only; educational and research use count as non-commercial. See the [license section of the Python package](https://github.com/birdnet-team/birdnet#license). For details on each model (sample rates, segment lengths, embedding sizes), see the [models page of the Python package](https://birdnet-team.github.io/birdnet/models.html).

### `birdnet_list_models()`

Each model comes in several variants. `birdnet_list_models()` lists every variant the installed `birdnet` Python package can load. `compact = TRUE` puts the precisions and libraries of otherwise identical rows into one string:

```{r list_models}
birdnet_list_models(compact = TRUE)
#>        type  version backend          needs      precision library
#> 8  acoustic      2.4      pb             tf           fp32    <NA>
#> 3  acoustic      2.4      tf           base fp16:fp32:int8  litert
#> 13 acoustic      2.4      tf             tf fp16:fp32:int8  tflite
#> 1  acoustic      3.0    onnx           base      fp16:fp32    <NA>
#> 10 acoustic      3.0      pb             tf           fp32    <NA>
#> 6  acoustic      3.0      pt             pt           fp32    <NA>
#> 5  acoustic      3.0      tf           base      fp16:fp32  litert
#> 15 acoustic      3.0      tf             tf      fp16:fp32  tflite
#> 12 acoustic perch_v2      pb             tf           fp32    <NA>
#> 9       geo      2.4      pb             tf           fp32    <NA>
#> 4       geo      2.4      tf           base           fp32  litert
#> 14      geo      2.4      tf             tf           fp32  tflite
#> 2       geo      3.0    onnx           base      fp16:fp32    <NA>
#> 11      geo      3.0      pb             tf           fp32    <NA>
#> 7       geo      3.0      pt             pt           fp32    <NA>
#> 16      geo      3.0      tf tf (2.18-2.19) fp16:fp32:int8  tflite
```

The columns match the arguments of `birdnet_load()`:

- `type`: `"acoustic"` (audio) or `"geo"` (location and week).
- `version`: `"3.0"`, `"2.4"`, or `"perch_v2"`. Load Perch with `birdnet_load_perch()`, everything else with `birdnet_load()`.
- `backend`: the format of the model file and the software that runs it.
  - `"onnx"`: ONNX Runtime. The default for V3.0.
  - `"tf"`: a TensorFlow Lite file. The default for V2.4. CPU only.
  - `"pb"`: a TensorFlow SavedModel (Protobuf). Can run on a GPU.
  - `"pt"`: PyTorch. Can run on a GPU.
- `library`: only for `backend = "tf"`, the interpreter for the TensorFlow Lite file. `"litert"` (Google's LiteRT) is part of the default installation; `"tflite"` is TensorFlow's own interpreter. birdnetR uses LiteRT on every platform that has it. LiteRT is not available on Intel Macs and Windows on ARM.
- `precision`: how precisely the model's numbers are stored. `"fp32"` is the full model. `"fp16"` and `"int8"` are smaller and can be faster, and their scores can differ slightly from `"fp32"`.
- `needs`: what the variant needs on top of the default installation.
  - `"base"`: nothing, it runs out of the box.
  - `"tf"`: TensorFlow (about 600 MB).
  - `"pt"`: PyTorch (several GB with GPU support, much less for the CPU-only version). On Linux, uv picks the CUDA build of torch by default; for the CPU-only build run `Sys.setenv(UV_TORCH_BACKEND = "cpu")` before the first birdnetR call.
  - `"tf (2.18-2.19)"`: TensorFlow 2.18 or 2.19 exactly. birdnetR's automatic install picks the newest TensorFlow, so this variant only works in a Python environment you manage yourself.

For example:

```{r load_variants}
birdnet_load(version = "2.4", precision = "int8")  # needs: base
birdnet_load(backend = "pt")                       # needs: pt
birdnet_load(type = "geo", version = "2.4", backend = "pb")  # needs: tf
```

When a variant needs TensorFlow or PyTorch, birdnetR installs it automatically the first time you load the model, also in the middle of an R session. Expect a longer wait that one time. There is one exception: if you point `RETICULATE_PYTHON` at your own Python environment, birdnetR can't install anything into it. Install `birdnet[tf]` or `birdnet[pt]` there yourself. See the [Troubleshoot](Troubleshoot.html) article for details, and for running models on a GPU.


## Next steps

Once you have predictions, you may want to filter, visualise, or validate them.
The [birdnetTools](https://birdnet-team.github.io/birdnetTools/index.html)
package provides functions for these tasks: filtering detections by species,
confidence, or date range; creating heatmaps; and running interactive validation
workflows to set species-specific confidence thresholds.

For processing many files, saving results, and handing them to birdnetTools,
see the [BirdNET ecosystem workflow](workflow.html) article.
